title: Count connected components with DSU
prompt: Implement countComponents(n int, edges [][]int) int: n nodes labelled 0..n-1 and an undirected edge list. Return how many connected components there are, using a disjoint set union rather than a traversal.
explanation: Start with n components and drop the count by one on every union that actually joins two different roots. Duplicate or redundant edges find the same root and are skipped, which is why you must compare roots before merging rather than counting edges. Path compression in find plus union by rank keeps each operation effectively constant.
hints: You never need to build an adjacency list. What is the answer before you have processed any edge?
Only an edge that joins two different roots changes the count.

title: A prefix tree with insert, search and startsWith
prompt: Fill in the Trie: Insert(word), Search(word) reporting whether the exact word was inserted, and StartsWith(prefix) reporting whether any inserted word begins with prefix. Words are lowercase a-z.
explanation: Search and StartsWith walk the identical path; the only difference is that Search additionally demands the end flag on the node it lands on. Factoring the walk into one helper is what stops the two from drifting apart. The end flag is also why 'app' can be a word while 'appl' is only a prefix.
hints: Search and StartsWith do the same descent. What single extra check separates them?
A node existing means some word passes through it. Something else has to mark where a word stops.
refs: LC 211 Design Add and Search Words

title: Course schedule with Kahn's algorithm
prompt: Implement canFinish(numCourses int, prerequisites [][]int) bool. Each pair {a, b} means you must take b before a. Return whether all courses can be finished, i.e. whether the dependency graph is acyclic. Use indegrees and a queue, not recursion.
explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly takes a course with nothing left blocking it and relaxes its dependents. Everything that never reaches indegree zero is stuck inside a cycle, so comparing the number emitted against numCourses is the cycle test: you get the ordering and the detection from one pass. Note the edge direction, {a, b} means b -> a, and getting it backwards still passes the symmetric cases.
hints: Count how many prerequisites each course is still waiting on, then start from the ones waiting on nothing.
You do not need to find the cycle. Compare how many courses you managed to emit with how many exist.

title: Sliding window maximum with a monotonic deque
prompt: Implement maxSlidingWindow(nums []int, k int) []int returning the maximum of every window of size k, left to right. O(n) overall: no re-scanning the window, and no heap.
explanation: The deque holds indices whose values decrease from front to back, so the front is always the current window's maximum. A new value evicts every smaller value behind it because those can never be the max again while the newcomer is in the window. Store indices, not values, or you cannot tell when the front has slid out of range.
hints: Keep candidates in the order they could still become the answer. What makes an older element permanently useless?
Two evictions per step: one from the back for being too small, one from the front for being too old.
refs: LC 862 Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
